extracted.intended_audience: aspiring comedy writers and general readers interested in comedy-writing craft and the TV/movie comedy industry
extracted.subtask_short: comedy writing advice and industry realities
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted criteria and practical takeaways about writing comedy (especially for TV/movies) drawn from a Slate book review of Mike Sacks’ Poking a Dead Frog; covers craft tips, writers' room dynamics, production pressures, and industry pitfalls. Useful for people learning how to produce comedy or evaluate what it takes to succeed in comedy-writing careers.

rubrics_metrics.name: You cannot teach someone how to be funny
rubrics_metrics.description: “The bottom line is you cannot teach someone how to be funny.” (statement repeated in the book; many interviewees make this point.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat instruction as limited: the book offers many interviews but not a manual on 'how to be funny.' Expect that formal tips will be vague, contradictory, or ornamental rather than prescriptive. Anti-pattern: approaching the book (or any single source) as a definitive comedy manual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Just keep writing (common exhortation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple exhortations such as Diablo Cody’s “Just keep writing.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize this as frequent, concise advice but largely a bumper-sticker: useful as encouragement but insufficient on its own. Combine with concrete practices (e.g., regular output, experimentation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewriting is writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Mel Brooks: “Rewriting is writing. It’s everything.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat rewriting as an essential part of craft—iterative polishing is a legitimate production method. Anti-pattern: assuming a first-draft flash of inspiration is a finished product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard work/sustained effort does not guarantee success
rubrics_metrics.description: James Downey: “You can spend hours and hours and focus and hard work and pain, and a piece will still not be good.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that persistence is necessary but not sufficient; be prepared to discard material and accept unpredictability. Do not conflate effort with guaranteed quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual approaches to comedy vary (poetry vs. math)
rubrics_metrics.description: Terry Jones likens comedy to the ineffable magic of poetry; Tom Scharpling calls comedy a cold, hard “math problem.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge multiple valid frameworks: some writers emphasize essence and ineffability, others view joke craft as pattern recognition and formula. Adopt or blend a framework that fits your process—there is no single correct definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writers’ room is the production engine and training ground
rubrics_metrics.description: The book emphasizes the writers’ room as an 'alchemical' space—a combination of gladiatorial arena, group therapy, and a production bunker—essential to producing and refining material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use collaborative rooms to generate volume, get instant feedback, and refine jokes; cultivate interpersonal dynamics and learn to make a room laugh. Scoring note: entry into a strong writers’ room is presented as a major career accelerator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television comedy requires factory-like output (quantity and consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: TV requires huge amounts of new content and the system 'has to run like a factory,' with writers expected to produce at 'the rate and consistency of an assembly-line worker.' (Dan Guterman)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize consistent productivity and the ability to produce many joke ideas under deadline. Anti-pattern: clinging to solitary artistry that prevents meeting production volume needs for TV.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and inhabit your role in the writers’ room
rubrics_metrics.description: Kay Cannon: 'You are sharing 14 hours a day with the same people... You need to learn what role you play every single day in that configuration.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and perform the role that best helps the room function (idea generator, editor, laugh-testing, etc.). Social fit and daily contribution matter as much as raw talent in a collaborative room.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy is a business—expect commerce to shape creative choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Mike Schur: 'It’s really where the rubber meets the road—the rubber being art and the road being commerce.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be pragmatic about compromises required by production, executives, advertisers, and audience expectations. Anti-pattern: insisting that high theory or lofty ideals will determine success in commercial environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for intense stress, insane deadlines, and precarious conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional comedy writers face 'insane deadlines, fickle audiences, humorless executives, and the constant threat of abject failure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop resilience and practical coping strategies; recognize the mental-health and financial strains of the job. Scoring note: stamina and tolerance for stress are implicit criteria for surviving as a professional comedy writer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic realities: freelancing, low pay, precarity, and labor disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: The industry increasingly relies on freelancers, non-union employees, and precariously employed writers; example: Fashion Police writers’ strike over pay and conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan financially and professionally for irregular pay and possible exploitation; consider unionization and labor protections. Career advice: 'If you can do anything else with your life and still be happy, do it.' (Andrés du Bouchet)

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity and representation matter in writers’ rooms
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer notes that out of 44 interviews in the book there are no people of color and only seven women, undermining the democratic ethos of writers’ rooms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value and recruit diverse voices; be aware that diversity programs (e.g., diversity staff writers) are responses to persistent underrepresentation. Anti-pattern: assuming meritocracy alone will yield equitable staffing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment with unconventional physical/mental techniques for idea generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Jack Handey wrote 'Deep Thoughts' by lying on the ground and repeatedly throwing a rubber ball at the ceiling; the reviewer adopted 'horizontal writing' and found it slightly helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try varied and personal routines (change posture, environment, ritual) to stimulate ideas; what works can be idiosyncratic. Scoring note: originality of method is less important than whether it reliably produces usable material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not romanticize comedy; be realistic about craft and outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: The book disabuses aspiring writers of romantic notions of comedy as 'search for truth' or timeless artistry—comedy is often hammered into a usable product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance appreciation for comedic art with an understanding of the industrialized, collaborative, and sometimes compromised process of creating television and film comedy. Anti-pattern: overvaluing historical/theoretical pedigree at the expense of practical production skills.
